To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

train, bus and car travel on dedicated busway, motorway or motorway on-ramp, and motorcyclists travel on motorway, are all associated with the lowest air pollution doses (CO concentrations x commute time x breathing rate).
the highest air pollution exposures are received by car commuters, while the lowest are received by train and busway commuters.
the highest exposures were received by motorcyclists and runners, followed by cyclists, with car commuters receiving lower levels of exposure than bus commuters.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and evaluation of a novel methodology to assess the air pollution exposures experienced by individuals travelling between specific start and end points by different modes of transport.
the development of an integrated model of air quality and health, and the application of this model to the development of a decision support system for transport planning in New Zealand.
the health effects of exposure to air pollution and how these are modified by the mode of transport and level of physical activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lowest exposures to air pollution are experienced by those travelling by train, and the highest exposures are experienced by those who travel by motorcycle.
travel by train and bus is the most effective in reducing air pollution exposure, with travel by car being the least effective.
the best way to minimise personal exposure to air pollution is to walk, cycle or run.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for a given level of activity, the air quality of the route is a key determinant of air pollution doses received.
the best options are to use the train and bus (especially when on dedicated busways).
for a typical Auckland commute, the best option for reducing air pollution exposure is to use the train.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of transport mode can make a significant difference in terms of the air pollution exposure received by the commuter.

, while there is no one best way to commute (in terms of personal exposure to air pollution), the results suggest that, for the majority of people, travel by train, bus or car on a dedicated busway would result in lower personal exposure to air pollutants compared with travel by car on congested roads.

, while there are some modes that are more effective than others in reducing personal exposures to air pollution (e.g., train, bus on busway), it is the combination of the level of physical exertion, commute time, and pollutant concentration that determines the air pollution dose.
